**Paederus (rove beetle) dermatitis** is the look-alike: toxin paederin, **linear and "kissing" lesions**.

sections.title: Overview
blocks: **Blister beetle dermatitis** is an acute irritant contact reaction to **cantharidin** in Meloidae beetles (e.g. *Lytta vesicatoria*, *Mylabris*). The beetle does **not** bite — lesions follow crushing or brushing it on the skin, often at night near lights. It is uncommon in the UK and mainly seen in travellers or outdoor workers from endemic regions.
**Paederus (rove beetle) dermatitis** is the closely related look-alike taught alongside it. The toxin is **paederin**, producing linear and “kissing” lesions. Management overlaps heavily.

ul: Cantharidin breaks desmosomes → acantholysis and an intraepidermal blister with little dermal inflammation (usually no scarring). The same mechanism is used therapeutically on warts and molluscum.
Paederin from crushed *Paederus* beetles causes delayed linear erythema then vesicles/pustules.
**Ingesting** cantharidin (e.g. as a purported aphrodisiac) is systemically toxic — a medical emergency, not a skin problem.
**"It's shingles"**: linear lesions without dermatomal pain and with a beetle history point to Paederus.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: Beetle toxins **break the bonds between skin cells**, so the epidermis splits.

ul: Onset within hours to about 24–48 h; the patient often does not link the insect.
Vesicles/bullae on an erythematous base — often **linear or bizarre** where the beetle was wiped; “kissing” lesions in flexures favour Paederus.
**Burning or stinging** more than itch.
Exposed sites: face, neck, arms, lower legs; toxin can be finger-transferred to eyes or genitals.
Heals in about a week, sometimes with lasting pigmentation in skin of colour.

sections.title: Diagnosis and investigations
blocks: Clinical: burning blisters on exposed skin after possible beetle contact, travel, camping or night lights. Clusters of cases support the diagnosis. Swab only if secondary infection or HSV/impetigo is realistic.

ddx.f: Paederus more linear / kissing / pustular; Meloidae more cantharidin bullae.

ul: If a beetle lands on skin, **blow or flick it off — do not crush or swat**.
Wash promptly with soap and water; avoid touching eyes or genitals.
Cool compresses; leave small blisters intact; drain large tense bullae aseptically keeping the roof on.
Simple analgesia.
Short course of **potent topical corticosteroid** on inflamed non-facial skin (mild/moderate on face or flexures).
Antihistamine if itch; sedating at night if sleep is poor.
Secondary infection: treat as impetigo/cellulitis per NICE — no routine prophylactic antibiotics.

blocks.title: Prescribing limits and pitfalls
list: **Prevention**: Nets, screens, cover skin, shake bedding, lights off near open windows.

refer.t: Eye pain, redness, photophobia or reduced vision: irrigate and **same-day eye casualty**.
Extensive blistering, genital involvement, severe pain or systemic illness; returned traveller with fever.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: Eye pain, redness, photophobia or reduced vision → irrigate and **same-day eye casualty**.
Extensive blistering, genital involvement, severe pain or systemic illness.
Ingestion → A&E / NPIS (TOXBASE).
Returned traveller with fever — think beyond beetle dermatitis.
Secondary infection, eye involvement (Nairobi eye), post-inflammatory pigmentation.
Heals in 1–2 weeks.

pearls: Ask “Did it **burn** or itch?” Burning linear blisters after lights outdoors → beetle; itchy grouped papules → bites.
